# Diagnosing Asymmetric Braking Pull on New Tires

When a vehicle suddenly begins to pull left or right during braking—especially when that behavior seems random and switches sides—it usually points to an asymmetry in how force is distributed across the four corners of the chassis. Since you recently switched back to summer tires, the most likely culprit isn't your alignment or wheel balancing, but rather the transition period itself combined with residual debris on the road surface.

The sensation of "fighting back" during braking suggests that one set of wheels is generating significantly more friction than the others. If the car tugs left today and right tomorrow at the exact same spot, you are likely encountering variable traction coefficients rather than a mechanical fault in the suspension or brake hardware. Winter tires leave behind a layer of rubber residue and often microscopic sand particles embedded in the road surface during the first few days of summer driving. These contaminants can create micro-patches of high friction on an otherwise smooth asphalt surface.

If your car's weight transfer dynamics are sensitive—which they always are under hard braking—these unpredictable patches can cause the vehicle to grab unevenly. One side might hit a patch of concentrated winter debris while the other hits clean pavement, resulting in a sudden pull. Because these patches are random, the symptom appears inconsistent, mimicking a failing caliper or a bent control arm, even though the mechanical components remain sound.

Before assuming your new wheels and tires are defective, consider performing a controlled isolation test. While you mentioned checking tire pressure, ensure you are doing so with a high-quality gauge rather than relying on the stem valve reading, which can be inaccurate. Inflate all four tires to the exact same PSI specified on the driver's side door jamb sticker. Next, clean the tread of your new summer tires thoroughly using a stiff brush and hot water to remove any road film or sand residue from the winter season. This step is critical; mixing old, dirty winter rubber with new summer compounds can temporarily alter handling until the new tread breaks in.

If cleaning the tires and confirming pressure levels does not resolve the issue, then you must inspect the braking hardware for uneven pad wear or stuck caliper pistons. A malfunctioning caliper often fails to retract fully after a stop, causing one pad to drag slightly even when stationary. This drag creates heat buildup that can warp rotors over time, leading to pulsation and pulling during subsequent stops.

To diagnose this mechanically, you need to inspect the brake drums or rotors for lateral runout. Use a dial indicator mounted on a fixed point of the wheel hub to measure how much the rotor shifts as it spins. If the runout exceeds 0.002 inches (0.05 mm), the rotor is warped and should be resurfaced or replaced. Additionally, check the caliper slide pins for corrosion or lack of lubrication. Sticky slides prevent the caliper from floating correctly during braking force application, effectively locking the wheel into a fixed position relative to the tire contact patch.

While mechanical faults are less likely given your description of random directional changes, they cannot be ruled out without physical inspection. If you find that the issue persists after cleaning and pressure checks, visiting a professional for a brake system audit is necessary. They can perform a "brake bench test" or inspect the calipers while the vehicle is lifted to confirm whether any pistons are sticking or if there is uneven pad material thickness causing drag.
